If you take only two things from this series, take these.

1. **An instrument's frequencies are the [spectrum](glossary.qmd#spectrum) of an [operator].** The operator is the rule that takes a shape of the instrument, a bent string or a dented drumhead, and returns the force pulling it back. Its eigenvalues give the frequencies the instrument can make. The [Fourier series](glossary.qmd#fourier-series) is the simplest case: the spectrum of $-d^2/d\theta^2$ on a circle.
2. **A clear [pitch](glossary.qmd#pitch) means a nearly evenly spaced spectrum.** Whether the frequencies line up on whole-number multiples is decided by the operator and the instrument's shape. How you play it decides only how loud each frequency is, with one exception: a steady bow or breath can force a sound to repeat exactly, and then it has a pitch whatever the operator says.

[operator]: glossary.qmd#operator

## How to read this series

Choose how deep to go. Every page opens with a plain explanation and a demo; the equations come next, and the step-by-step derivations and proofs are folded away. Technical words link to the [glossary](glossary.qmd).

- **The gist, 5 minutes.** Stay on this page. Read the two points above, then play the instruments just below. Listen for which ones have a clear pitch, and compare their stems with the gray whole-number grid. The kalimba is the interesting case: its overtones are off the grid, but weak and brief.
- **The core idea, about 35 minutes.** Read [0 · What is a note?](note.qmd), [3 · The circle](circle.qmd), [4 · A string with ends](violin.qmd) and [8 · The drum](drum.qmd), skipping the folds. These four pages carry both points: a pitch is a repeating sound, the circle is the smallest operator and its spectrum, the string is a real instrument with an evenly spaced spectrum, and the drum is one without.
- **Every instrument, about an hour and a half.** Pages 0 to 8 in order.
- **Everything, about two and a half hours.** All the pages, including [9 · What the spectrum knows](shape.qmd), with the folds open.

Here for one instrument? Go straight to its page in the table of all pages below; each page says at the top which earlier page it builds on and how long it takes. Already know Fourier series? Start at page 4. Interested in spectral geometry? Read pages 3, 8 and 9 with the folds open. The times assume reading about 120 words a minute, plus a minute or two per demo.

## All pages

| Page | New idea | Operator | Frequencies |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| [0 · What is a note?](note.qmd) | a note is a sound that repeats; its partials are whole-number multiples | | $f, 2f, 3f, \dots$ |
| [1 · One mass on a spring](oscillator.qmd) | one restoring force, one frequency | the number $k/m$ | $\sqrt{k/m}/2\pi$ |
| [2 · Beads on a ring](ring.qmd) | many masses: eigenvectors of a matrix | circulant matrix | $\propto \sin(\pi k/N)$ |
| [3 · The circle](circle.qmd) | the smallest operator spectrum; Fourier series | $-d^2/d\theta^2$ on $L^2(S^1)$ | $\propto n$, exactly |
| [4 · A string with ends](violin.qmd) | boundary conditions are part of the operator | $-c^2\,d^2/dx^2$, ends tied | $\propto n$ |
| [5 · An air column](clarinet.qmd) | a different boundary condition removes half the spectrum | the same, on pressure | $\propto 2n - 1$ |
| [6 · Change the order](kalimba.qmd) | bending: four derivatives, scattered overtones | $\kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4$ | $1 : 6.27 : 17.55$ |
| [6b · The harmonica](harmonica.qmd) | the excitation, not the operator, can set the overtones | the same as 6 | heard as $\propto n$ |
| [7 · The piano](piano.qmd) | operators add; the pedals act on damping and forcing, not on the spectrum | $-c^2\partial_x^2 + \kappa^2\partial_x^4$ | $n\sqrt{1 + Bn^2}$ |
| [8 · The drum](drum.qmd) | two dimensions; no clear pitch | $-c^2\Delta$ on a disk | Bessel zeros |
| [9 · What the spectrum knows](shape.qmd) | the spectrum hears area and perimeter, not shape | $-\Delta$ on any region | Weyl's law |

: The ladder. {.striped}

## Families

<details><summary>Instruments that are the same up to constants</summary>

Instruments with the same operator and boundary conditions are the same mathematical object with different constants. Each family below shares one operator; the last column says what still differs inside it.

| Family | Operator and boundary | Demos | What varies inside the family |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Strings under tension | $-c^2\partial_x^2$, tied ends | [Violin](violin.qmd) | length, tension, mass per length; plucked (guitar, harp) or bowed (violin, cello) |
| Air columns | $-c^2\partial_x^2$ on pressure | [Clarinet](clarinet.qmd), with a flute switch | the boundary condition: one end closed (clarinet, pan pipes) or both open (flute) |
| Clamped bars | $\kappa^2\partial_x^4$, clamped base, free tip | [Kalimba](kalimba.qmd), [Harmonica](harmonica.qmd) | steel tine or brass reed; plucked or blown, which decides whether you hear harmonics |
| Stiff strings | $-c^2\partial_x^2 + \kappa^2\partial_x^4$, pinned ends | [Piano](piano.qmd) | stiffness, rising toward the treble |
| Membranes | $-c^2\Delta$ on a disk | [Drum](drum.qmd) | tension and size; the air under a timpani head |

</details>

## Comparison

<details><summary>Every instrument side by side: force, operator, boundary, eigen-condition, ratios, excitation</summary>

| | Violin | Clarinet | Kalimba | Harmonica | Piano | Drum |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Restoring force | tension | air pressure | bending | bending | tension + bending | tension, in 2D |
| Newton's law on | a segment | a slab of air | a slice: torque, then force | a slice, as for the kalimba | a segment, both forces added | a patch, via the divergence theorem |
| Operator | $-c^2\partial_x^2$ | $-c^2\partial_x^2$ on pressure | $\kappa^2\partial_x^4$ | $\kappa^2\partial_x^4$ | $-c^2\partial_x^2+\kappa^2\partial_x^4$ | $-c^2\Delta$ |
| Boundary | $u=0$ at both ends | $p_x=0$ at reed, $p=0$ at open end | $u=u'=0$ at clamp, $u''=u'''=0$ at tip | same as the kalimba | $u=u''=0$ at both ends | $u=0$ on the rim |
| Eigen-condition | $\sin kL=0$ | $\cos kL=0$ | $\cos\beta L\cosh\beta L=-1$ | $\cos\beta L\cosh\beta L=-1$ | $\sin kL=0$ | $J_m(ka)=0$ |
| Mode ratios | $n$ | $2n-1$ | 1, 6.27, 17.5 | 1, 6.27, 17.5 | $n\sqrt{(1+Bn^2)/(1+B)}$ | 1, 1.59, 2.14 |
| Excitation | bow, sustained | reed, sustained | thumb pluck | airflow, sustained | felt hammer | stick |
| What you hear | exact harmonics | odd harmonics dominate; overblows a twelfth | pitch plus a brief clink | exact harmonics, from the chopped airflow | near-harmonic; stretched octaves | inharmonic: a thud |

</details>

```{=html}
<script src="core.js"></script>
<script>
(function () {
  "use strict";
  var C = Core, M = C.models;
  var DEF = {
    violin: function () { return M.violin.partials(); },
    clarinet: function () { return M.clarinet.partials(); },
    kalimba: function () { return M.kalimba.partials(); },
    harmonica: function () { return M.harmonica.partials(); },
    piano: function () { return M.piano.partials({ B: 0.0012 }); },
    drum: function () { return M.drum.partials({ r: 0.35 }); }
  };
  var SUSTAINED = { violin: 1, clarinet: 1, harmonica: 1 };
  function draw() {
    document.querySelectorAll("svg[data-mini]").forEach(function (svg) {
      C.stems(svg, DEF[svg.getAttribute("data-mini")](), { W: 200, H: 58, rmax: 8, fs: 9, sw: 2, labelEvery: 2 });
    });
    document.querySelectorAll("[data-ratios]").forEach(function (el) {
      el.textContent = DEF[el.getAttribute("data-ratios")]().map(function (p) { return p.ratio; }).sort(function (a, b) { return a - b; }).slice(0, 4).map(function (r) { return r.toFixed(2); }).join(", ");
    });
  }
  function fadeOut(buf, sec) { var d = buf.getChannelData(0), n = Math.floor(sec * buf.sampleRate); for (var i = 0; i < n; i++) d[d.length - 1 - i] *= i / n; return buf; }
  document.querySelectorAll("[data-play]").forEach(function (b) {
    b.addEventListener("click", function () {
      var id = b.getAttribute("data-play"), f = M[id].F0, buf;
      if (SUSTAINED[id]) buf = fadeOut(C.render(C.toHz(DEF[id](), f), 1.8), 0.4);
      else buf = C.render(C.toHz(DEF[id](), f), id === "piano" ? 3.2 : 2.6);
      C.play(buf, 0.8);
    });
  });

  C.onTheme(draw);
  draw();
})();
</script>
```
